name: Bethel University: Classifieds (and Book Exchange)
summary: Campus classifieds web app run by Bethel University's in-house web/ITS team (private university, St. Paul MN). The same code also runs the university's Book Exchange. Flask + Flask-SQLAlchemy on SQLite, about 1.8k Python lines, 4 tables, 24 Jinja templates, CAS single sign-on through Apache.

evidence.text: PR #58 (merged 2026-10-23) pinned dependencies so the app runs on the team's OS 8 servers.
requirements.txt pins Flask==1.1.4, Werkzeug==1.0.1, Jinja2==2.11.3 and keeps the unmaintained Flask-Classy and Flask-Script.
Dependabot PR to bump Flask 1.1.4 to 3.1.3 (a security fix release), open since 2026-10-23.
Dependabot PR to bump Werkzeug 1.0.1 to 3.1.9 (a security fix release), open since 2026-10-23.
Config template points SQLAlchemy at a local SQLite file (app.db).
Cron script dumps the SQLite DB every 6 hours, keeps 13 days, and covers both the classifieds and book_exchange deployments.
Queries use LIKE against integer IDs and boolean columns. SQLite accepts this; PostgreSQL rejects it.
Flask-Script imports flask._compat, which was removed in Flask 2.0. The project is archived.

scope_fit: Strong. Small internal tool (about 1.8k Python lines, 4 tables: posts, contacts, categories, post_categories) on Flask-SQLAlchemy + SQLite. Server-rendered Jinja templates with one or two small JSON endpoints. Auth is Apache mod_auth_cas via REMOTE_USER. A nightly cron calls an expire handler, and email goes through smtplib. No tests. Two deployments (Classifieds and Book Exchange) share the code.
blockers: Server-rendered templates use Flask-Classy endpoint names (83 url_for calls) and need compatibility shims.
CAS hand-off: REMOTE_USER from Apache/mod_wsgi does not reach an ASGI app the same way.
The team may prefer Flask 3 to FastAPI (they have a Flask house style across several apps).
The database holds names, emails and phone numbers, so a sanitized copy or on-site migration is needed.
PostgreSQL may not be their standard (other Bethel apps use Oracle or MySQL).
University procurement and data-agreement steps.
access_path: Code is already public (no license file), so a full pre-assessment needs no access. For the pilot, Bethel would share the deployed commit and config (secrets removed) and the two SQLite files or their cron dumps, sanitized if needed.
contact_channel: Bethel ITS service portal https://bethel.topdesk.net (listed on https://www.bethel.edu/its/apps, which also gives a general help-desk email), asking for the request to be routed to the web applications team.

name: SizeSquirrel
summary: Public climbing-shoe sizing and deals site (sizesquirrel.com) with a Flask JSON API backend and a Vue front end. Maintained by its single owner, who says the site barely covers its costs and invites contributors.

evidence.text: requirements.txt pins Flask==1.1.4, Werkzeug==1.0.1, Flask-Script==2.0.6, SQLAlchemy==1.4.25 and Flask-SQLAlchemy==2.5.1.
README recommends Python 3.8.2 and Node 14.16 (both end-of-life) and says no new features are planned.
Development settings use a SQLite database; a sample dev database is committed.
The backend is a JSON API (apiv2 routes returning jsonify).
Management commands run through the archived Flask-Script.

scope_fit: Near-ideal technically: JSON API, Flask-SQLAlchemy with 5 models (user, gender, brand, item, user_item), about 4k Python lines (excluding about 100 data-only Alembic migrations), own user auth, batch scripts for affiliate data feeds. No tests. The production DB engine is not stated.
blockers: Very limited budget (the owner says the site barely pays its costs).
Production database engine unverified (only the dev config shows SQLite).
Shoe catalogue data lives in Alembic data migrations, so migration history must be preserved.
Batch jobs depend on Flask-Script and need re-homing.
access_path: Code and a sample development database are public, so a public sample assessment needs no access. A real pilot would need the production DB from the owner.
contact_channel: GitHub issues on eddieferrer/sizesquirrel-open (the README invites discussion there).

name: Isso
summary: Widely used self-hosted comment server (Disqus alternative): a JSON API with hand-written SQL on raw sqlite3. Maintained by the isso-comments GitHub organisation; release 0.14.0 in March 2026.

evidence.text: Issue #61, opened in 2014 by the original author, asks for a SQL abstraction layer so MySQL and PostgreSQL can be used. Still open, labelled needs-contributor and needs-decision. Third-party Postgres and MySQL forks are linked in the thread.
Database layer uses raw sqlite3 connections and hand-written SQL.
The app is built on Werkzeug routing and middleware, not Flask.
An AI policy added 2026-10-25 requires a human copyright owner for each contribution and bans unsupervised agentic tools.

scope_fit: Partial. JSON API, raw sqlite3, about 4 tables, roughly 4-5k Python lines with tests (good). But it is Werkzeug, not Flask; upstream would want an optional PostgreSQL backend rather than a FastAPI rewrite; it sends email/webhook notifications.
blockers: Not a Flask app (Werkzeug), so it sits outside the literal v1 job.
No built-in payer; a paid job would come from a site operator, who would then maintain a fork.
The project's AI policy restricts agent-made contributions upstream.
Maintainers value SQLite simplicity.
access_path: Code is public, enough for a public sample assessment. A paying site operator would provide their comments database.
contact_channel: GitHub Discussions https://github.com/isso-comments/isso/discussions or IRC #isso on Libera.Chat (both listed in the README).

name: Wavect GmbH
summary: Austrian custom-software agency (Ampass, Tyrol and Vienna) run by two founders with a specialist network. A possible partner or subcontracting channel for client Flask apps.

evidence.text: The agency's own site has a dedicated Flask development page: building Flask services, making existing ones easier to run and change, checking extension compatibility, testing API behaviour.
The homepage describes a two-founder company working with a network of specialists.

scope_fit: Partner channel rather than a direct customer. They could pass along client Flask + SQLite apps that need a fixed-scope FastAPI + PostgreSQL upgrade, with Goose delivering the mechanical part and its test evidence. No evidence about SQLite usage among their clients.
blockers: The agency may prefer to do upgrade work itself.
Its Flask page is about keeping Flask services, not migrating away from Flask.
No proof of client demand for this specific job.
access_path: Client code and databases would come through the agency under its client agreements.
last_activity: Website live when checked on 2026-11-04 (no dated post checked)

name: Level 12
summary: Custom software consultancy in Louisville, KY that presents its team as Python developers first and has worked since 2011. Its official GitHub organisation maintains Keg, a Flask + SQLAlchemy framework.

evidence.text: Keg, a framework built on Flask and SQLAlchemy, is maintained in the company's GitHub org (profile links to level12.io), pushed 2026-09-02.
GitHub org activity continues in late 2026 (e.g. flask-hypergen pushed 2026-11-03).
Blog post (2025-04-25) on AI-assisted updating of a Python library.
Caveat: the homepage and blog index do not mention Flask; the Flask evidence comes from the company's own GitHub org.

scope_fit: Weak as a channel for a FastAPI-only offer. Their Flask framework (Keg) is part of their identity, and they already use AI tools for modernisation work.
blockers: A FastAPI-only offer competes with their own Flask framework.
They may see Goose as a competitor.
Unknown whether their client apps use SQLite.
access_path: Referral or subcontract; client code and data would come through Level 12.

name: Subscribie
summary: Open-source subscription-payments platform with a hosted service (subscribie.co.uk) for small businesses. Built on Flask + Flask-SQLAlchemy with SQLite by default.

evidence.text: Issue #738, opened in 2021 by the project's lead contributor and still open, asks for migrations to work on MySQL as groundwork for higher-availability databases without a single point of failure.
Matching PR #898 has been open since 2022, last updated 2023-03-30.
The default settings example uses a SQLite database.

scope_fit: Out of v1 range by size. About 13k Python lines and 148 HTML templates (server-rendered), Stripe payments, uWSGI multi-instance hosting. Modern Python (>=3.12). The stated target DB is MySQL, not PostgreSQL.
blockers: Size and template count well above the v1 guideline.
Payment flows (Stripe) raise risk.
The maintainer's target is MySQL rather than PostgreSQL.
They would probably want to stay on Flask.
access_path: Code is public. Shop databases are held by the operator.
contact_channel: GitHub issues on Subscribie/subscribie (the hosted-service site mentions email/chat support but has no contact page).

name: OpenAlgo
summary: Self-hosted algorithmic-trading platform with 36 broker plugins, maintained by Marketcalls (Bangalore). Flask 3 with several SQLite databases plus DuckDB.

evidence.text: Issue #2355 (opened 2026-11-03): on the default SQLite DB, the APScheduler thread crashes with 'database is locked' and all scheduled flows stop until a restart.
Earlier report of background schedulers leaking SQLite read locks (closed Aug 2026).
Fresh-install scheduler failures with 'database is locked' (closed Aug 2026).
Sample env defines five separate SQLite databases plus a DuckDB file.

scope_fit: Far beyond v1: over 1,200 Python files outside tests, Flask-RESTX API, Socket.IO, APScheduler, multiple databases. They would need PostgreSQL support added rather than a FastAPI migration.
blockers: Codebase size.
Real-money trading risk.
Many self-hosted installs, each with its own databases.
Already on modern Flask 3.1.3, so a framework change is not wanted.
access_path: Code is public. Each trader holds their own databases; work would need the maintainer's buy-in.
contact_channel: GitHub issues on marketcalls/openalgo, or the Discord server linked in the README.

name: MakeIt Labs authbackend
summary: Membership, billing and RFID access-control backend of MakeIt Labs, a 501(c)(3) makerspace in Nashua, NH. Flask with SQLite in production.

evidence.text: Repo description: membership and authorisation backend with web interface, API and Stripe billing, supporting the space's access-control devices.
README describes restoring the production SQLite databases from S3 backups and calls its own docs rough as of April 2022.
requirements.txt pins 2022-era packages: Flask==2.0.2, Werkzeug==2.0.2, Flask-User==1.0.2.2, SQLAlchemy==1.4.31, oauth2client, slacker.
Raw SQL schema file alongside Flask-SQLAlchemy usage.
Charity Navigator lists MakeIt Labs (Nashua, NH) as a 501(c)(3).

scope_fit: Too large for v1. About 18k Python lines, 84 templates, mixed raw sqlite3 and Flask-SQLAlchemy, plus an MQTT daemon, Slack integration, nightly jobs, Google OAuth, Stripe and S3 backups.
blockers: Size and number of integrations.
Door-access hardware depends on it.
Member personal data.
Volunteer-run with a small budget.
No repo activity since January 2024.
access_path: Code is public. Volunteers would need to approve sharing a (sanitized) copy of the member database.
contact_channel: MakeIt Labs contact page https://makeitlabs.com/contact or GitHub issues on makeitlabs/authbackend.
last_activity: 2024-01-26 (last push and issue #49); last default-branch commit 2022-12-29
